summary: Moon–Mars Analog Finder is a web tool that shows where on Earth a team can rehearse work planned for permanent Moon bases and Mars sites. We divided Earth's land into 88,883 cells of 0.5° (about 55 km) and gave every cell, and each of 12 targets (5 at the lunar south pole, 7 on Mars), the same measures built from NASA data: terrain at a 1 km step, cold, ground ice, bare ground, snow-free months, minerals, volcanoes, impact structures and dryness. For each of seven test tasks, such as landing, rover mobility, EVA geology or ice mining, a cell scores higher the closer its measures are to the target's. The page ranks the best regions, explains every score, lets users change weights and filters, and lists what Earth cannot reproduce (gravity, radiation, pressure, extreme cold) beside each candidate. Analog campaigns are costly and sites are often chosen by tradition. A transparent, data-based ranking helps agencies, universities and students find new places to test.
details: Moon–Mars Analog Finder answers one question: where on Earth can a crew best rehearse work planned for a Moon or Mars base? A Python pipeline builds "fingerprints" of 12 targets (5 at the lunar south pole, 7 on Mars) from NASA PDS data (LRO LOLA and Diviner, MGS MOLA, Mars Odyssey GRS). It measures 88,883 Earth land cells (0.5°, about 55 km) the same way, using SRTMGL30, MODIS temperature, vegetation and snow, EMIT minerals, NASA POWER precipitation, and volcano and impact-structure lists. Terrain of all three worlds is compared at the same 1 km step. Each of seven test tasks (landing, rover mobility, EVA geology, ice mining, low-Sun operations, caves, biosignatures) has its own weights and hard filters. The result is one static web page where scoring runs in the browser, so users change weights and filters and the map re-ranks at once. Low Sun depends only on latitude and season, so we keep it out of the score and show it as a window: hours a day with the Sun 0–5° up in a snow-free month, and which month. Weights are set by hand, not tuned on known sites. Against 32 known analog sites the median percentile is 0.78 (random: 0.50); without the two tasks whose lists contain the sites themselves it is 0.67, and the page says so. It also lists what Earth cannot reproduce next to every candidate. Built with Python, JavaScript (canvas), Docker/Caddy and GitHub Actions, in English and Ukrainian. Claude (Anthropic) helped to write the code and docs from our plan; the team chose targets, tasks and weights and reviewed the results.
